title_en: Wu Kai v. Zhu Chao and Shuguang School — dispute over compensation for personal injury
ruling_gist_en: I. According to Article 16 of the General Principles of the Civil Law and Article 22 of the Opinions of the Supreme People's Court on Several Issues concerning the Implementation of the General Principles of the Civil Law of the People's Republic of China (for Trial Implementation), when a guardian sends a minor student to school for study, the guardian's guardianship duties are not transferred to the school; nor does the school automatically assume guardianship duties over the student simply by accepting the minor student for study. If the guardian wishes to delegate part or all of the guardianship duties to the school, a clear delegation agreement must be reached with the school. In the absence of a clear delegation agreement, it cannot be presumed that the school has accepted the guardian's delegation and assumed part or all of the guardianship duties over the minor student studying at the school.

full_text_en:
Wu Kai v. Zhu Chao, Shuguang School — dispute over compensation for personal injury

【Ruling Summary】

1. According to Article 16 of the General Principles of the Civil Law of the People's Republic of China and Article 22 of the Supreme People's Court's Opinions on Several Issues concerning the Implementation of the General Principles of the Civil Law of the People's Republic of China (for Trial Implementation), when a guardian sends a minor student to school for study, the guardian's custodial duties are not transferred to the school; nor does the school automatically assume custodial duties over the student simply by accepting the minor student for study at the school. If the guardian wishes to delegate part or all of the custodial duties to the school, the guardian must reach a clear agreement on such delegation with the school. Without a clear delegation agreement, it cannot be presumed that the school has accepted the guardian's entrustment and assumed part or all of the custodial duties over the minor student studying at the school.

2. According to Article 7 of the Supreme People's Court's Interpretation on Several Issues concerning the Application of Law in the Trial of Cases Involving Compensation for Personal Injury, although a school does not have custodial duties over minor students studying at the school, it does have the duty to educate, manage, and protect them. If the school fails to properly perform its duties of education, management, and protection, resulting in a minor student injuring another minor student on campus, then in addition to the liability of the guardian of the tortfeasor, the school shall also bear compensation liability corresponding to its fault.

Plaintiff: Wu Kai, male, 8 years old, student, residing at Suzui Town, Chuzhou District, Huai'an City, Jiangsu Province.

Legal Representative: Wu Fucheng, father of the plaintiff Wu Kai.

Defendant: Zhu Chao, male, 7 years old, student, residing at Zhuqiao Town, Chuzhou District, Huai'an City, Jiangsu Province.

Legal Representative: Zhu Shanyong, father of the defendant Zhu Chao.

Defendant: Jiangsu Huai'an Shuguang Bilingual School, domiciled at Jianhuai Township, Chuzhou District, Huai'an City, Jiangsu Province.

Legal Representative: Ding Deli, principal of the school.

The plaintiff, Wu Kai, brought an action for compensation for personal injury against the defendant Zhu Chao and the defendant Jiangsu Huai'an Shuguang Bilingual School (hereinafter referred to as Shuguang School), represented by his father Wu Fucheng, before the Chuzhou District People's Court of Huai'an City, Jiangsu Province. Zhu Chao's father, Zhu Shanyong, represented Zhu Chao in responding to the action.

Plaintiff's Allegations: While the plaintiff was resting in the dormitory of the defendant Shuguang School, his right eye was injured by an orange thrown by the defendant Zhu Chao. After treatment at several hospitals, the plaintiff still suffers from a disability. Shuguang School owes custodial duties to the plaintiff. Since the plaintiff was injured while studying and living at the school, Shuguang School should compensate the plaintiff for his losses. Zhu Chao is the direct tortfeasor and should also bear compensation liability. However, Shuguang School and Zhu Chao have been shifting responsibility onto each other and refusing to bear compensation liability. The plaintiff requests the court to order Shuguang School and Zhu Chao to pay the plaintiff medical expenses of RMB 39,056.76, nursing fees of RMB 12,000, hospital meal expenses of RMB 180, nutrition expenses of RMB 249.37, accommodation expenses of RMB 1,500, transportation expenses of RMB 3,996, disability compensation of RMB 9,507.80, moral damages of RMB 5,000, appraisal fees of RMB 300, and lost schooling expenses of RMB 1,208, and to bear the litigation costs of this case.

Defendant Zhu Chao's Defense: Zhu Chao is a person without capacity for civil conduct. During the school period, his parents were unable to perform their custodial duties over him, and the custodial duties were transferred to the school. The defendant Shuguang School operates a closed management system and owes custodial duties to boarding students. Therefore, it should bear compensation liability for the injury suffered by the plaintiff while at school. In addition, after the plaintiff was injured, Shuguang School failed to provide proper treatment, delayed medical care, and aggravated the losses. For these reasons, it should also bear liability.

Defendant Shuguang School's Defense: According to the law, the guardians of a minor are his parents, and only the guardians owe custodial duties to the minor. Custodial duties cannot be arbitrarily transferred to a school. The plaintiff Wu Kai was injured by the act of the defendant Zhu Chao, and the school provided timely assistance after the injury. The school has fully performed its duties of protection, care, and management over the boarding students and was not at fault for the injury suffered by the plaintiff. Therefore, it should not bear compensation liability. Furthermore, among the statutory items of compensation for personal injury, there is no item for "lost schooling expenses." The plaintiff's claim against the school should be dismissed.

The Chuzhou District People's Court of Huai'an City found the following facts after trial:

The defendant Shuguang School is a private boarding elementary school that implements a closed management system for its students. On June 13, 2004, the guardians of the plaintiff Wu Kai and the defendant Zhu Chao respectively signed enrollment agreements with Shuguang School, enrolling Wu Kai and Zhu Chao in the school. In September of the same year, Wu Kai and Zhu Chao became students in Class 1, Grade 1 of Shuguang School and shared the same dormitory. At approximately 10:00 p.m. on December 17, 2004, while Wu Kai and Zhu Chao were resting on their respective beds in the dormitory, Zhu Chao threw an orange that struck Wu Kai's right eye, causing injury. Wu Kai cried after being injured. A teacher discovered the situation and immediately sent Wu Kai to the school clinic for treatment. At the end of December, Shuguang School notified Wu Kai's parents of his injury. Wu Kai's parents took him to Jianhu Jianyang Eye Hospital, Huai'an First People's Hospital, Huai'an Second People's Hospital, and the Eye, Ear, Nose, and Throat Hospital affiliated with Fudan University for treatment. The total medical expenses amounted to RMB 39,592.58, transportation expenses RMB 2,040, and accommodation expenses RMB 1,000. For Wu Kai's treatment, Zhu Chao's guardian paid RMB 561.60 in advance, and Shuguang School paid RMB 10,000 in advance.

According to forensic medical appraisal, Wu Kai's right eye suffered from blunt trauma, vitreous hemorrhage, and retinal detachment, resulting in low vision level 1 of the right eye, constituting a Class 10 disability; Wu Kai required nutritional supplementation for one month after the injury and nursing care for three to four months after the injury; the medications used after the injury were all clinically appropriate symptomatic treatments for trauma patients, with no obvious impropriety. Both parties had no objection to the foregoing forensic conclusions, nor to the appraisal fee of RMB 300, hospital meal expenses of RMB 180, nutrition expenses of RMB 249.37, and disability compensation of RMB 9,508 due to Wu Kai.

The above facts are confirmed by the parties' statements, the enrollment agreements, medical records and relevant receipts for medical expenses, transportation expenses, accommodation expenses, appraisal fees, as well as investigation records, certificates, appraisal reports, and other evidence.

The issues in dispute in this case are: 1. Whether a school bears custodial duties over minor students during their study and life at school? 2. Who should bear liability for the injury in this case? 3. Is the plaintiff's claim for compensation for lost schooling expenses reasonable?

The Chuzhou District People's Court of Huai'an City held:

I. Article 16 of the General Principles of the Civil Law of the People's Republic of China (hereinafter referred to as the General Principles of the Civil Law) provides: "The parents of a minor are the guardians of the minor. If the parents of a minor are deceased or lack the capacity to be guardians, the following persons, who have the capacity to be guardians, shall act as guardians: (1) paternal or maternal grandparents; (2) elder brothers or sisters; (3) other close relatives or friends who are willing to bear the responsibility of guardianship and have obtained the consent of the minor's parents' work unit or the neighborhood committee or villagers' committee of the minor's place of residence. If there is a dispute over the designation of a guardian, the minor's parents' work unit or the neighborhood committee or villagers' committee of the minor's place of residence shall designate a guardian among the minor's close relatives. If a party brings a lawsuit challenging the designation, the people's court shall make a ruling. If none of the persons listed in the first and second paragraphs is available to be the guardian, the minor's parents' work unit or the neighborhood committee or villagers' committee of the minor's place of residence or the civil affairs department shall act as the guardian." Accordingly, guardianship is a civil right based on status. Only when a minor has no parents or other relatives to act as guardians can the minor's parents' work unit or the neighborhood committee, villagers' committee, civil affairs department, or other such units of the minor's place of residence become the guardian. A school cannot become the guardian of a minor. The law clearly defines the scope of guardians, and guardianship relationships are not to be arbitrarily established or changed. Therefore, when a guardian sends a minor student to school for study, the guardian's custodial duties are not transferred to the school; nor does the school automatically assume custodial duties over the student simply by accepting the minor student for study at the school. Article 22 of the Supreme People's Court's Opinions on Several Issues concerning the Implementation of the General Principles of the Civil Law of the People's Republic of China (for Trial Implementation) provides: "A guardian may delegate part or all of the custodial duties to another person. If civil liability arises due to the tortious act of the ward, the guardian shall bear the liability, unless otherwise agreed; if the delegate is actually at fault, he shall bear joint and several liability." This provision establishes that custodial duties may be transferred through delegation. If a guardian wishes to delegate part or all of the custodial duties to a school, the guardian must reach a clear agreement on such delegation with the school. Without a clear delegation agreement, it cannot be presumed that the school has accepted the guardian's entrustment and assumed part or all of the custodial duties over the minor student studying at the school.

In this case, the defendant Shuguang School is a private boarding elementary school. Compared with other day-school schools, a boarding elementary school merely has an expanded scope of internal management; it does not change the essential nature of the school's duty to educate, manage, and protect its students. Moreover, changes in a school's internal management do not necessarily result in the transfer of custodial duties over minor students. In the enrollment agreement signed between Shuguang School and the student's parents, there was no stipulation that the parents entrusted the school to perform custodial duties over the minor student. Therefore, regarding the minor students studying at the school, Shuguang School does not have custodial duties.

II. In this case, the plaintiff Wu Kai was resting in the dormitory of the defendant Shuguang School when his right eye was injured by an orange thrown by the defendant Zhu Chao. Article 133 of the General Principles of the Civil Law provides: "If a person without capacity for civil conduct or a person with limited capacity for civil conduct causes damage to another person, the guardian shall bear civil liability. If the guardian has fulfilled his guardianship duties, his civil liability may be appropriately reduced." The tortfeasor Zhu Chao is a person without capacity for civil conduct. Since Zhu Chao caused injury to another, Zhu Chao's guardian is naturally the subject of compensation according to law. Article 7 of the Supreme People's Court's Interpretation on Several Issues concerning the Application of Law in the Trial of Cases Involving Compensation for Personal Injury provides: "If a school, kindergarten, or other educational institution that bears the duty to educate, manage, and protect minors fails to perform its relevant duties within the scope of its responsibilities, resulting in personal injury to a minor, or a minor causing personal injury to another person, the institution shall bear compensation liability corresponding to its fault. If a third party's tort causes personal injury to a minor, the tortfeasor shall bear compensation liability. If a school, kindergarten, or other educational institution is at fault, it shall bear corresponding supplementary compensation liability." Although Shuguang School does not have custodial duties over minor students at the school, it does have the duty to educate, manage, and protect them. In performing its duties of education, management, and protection, if Shuguang School is without fault, it would not be a subject bearing liability in this case; if it is at fault, it would become another subject bearing liability in this case, bearing compensation liability corresponding to its fault. Wu Kai was injured at approximately 10:00 p.m. on December 17, 2004, which was already past the time for boarding students to turn off lights and go to sleep. According to Shuguang School's management system, the teachers specifically responsible for student life should patrol the dormitories to check on the minor students' sleeping conditions. The facts show that Wu Kai, Zhu Chao, and others had not fallen asleep beyond the stipulated time. Shuguang School failed to promptly discover and manage this abnormal situation, leading to a preventable injury accident. After the injury accident occurred, Shuguang School not only failed to provide timely and effective treatment to Wu Kai but also delayed notifying his guardians of the injury for more than ten days, thereby aggravating Wu Kai's condition. Shuguang School did not fully perform its duties of education, management, and protection over the minor students and was subjectively at fault to a certain extent. Therefore, it should naturally become another subject bearing liability in this case.

Article 133 of the General Principles of the Civil Law provides that for the tortious act of a person without capacity for civil conduct, the guardian bears liability without fault; if the guardian has fulfilled his guardianship duties, his civil liability may be appropriately reduced. Article 7 of the Supreme People's Court's Interpretation on Several Issues concerning the Application of Law in the Trial of Cases Involving Compensation for Personal Injury provides that in campus injury cases, the school bears civil liability corresponding to its fault. The plaintiff Wu Kai was injured while living at the defendant Shuguang School and was not at fault himself; the defendant Zhu Chao committed the injuring act, but Zhu Chao is a minor and injured another person while at school. Whether to the tortfeasor or the victim, Shuguang School owes duties of education, management, and protection. Shuguang School's failure to fully perform these duties is the main cause of the injury accident in this case. Shuguang School's subjective fault is relatively significant and should bear primary compensation liability for the injury consequences. Because Shuguang School implements a closed management system, Zhu Chao's guardian's performance of custodial duties was restricted. Although the guardian of Zhu Chao is not at fault for Zhu Chao's tortious act, he should still bear liability, but should bear secondary liability. The plaintiff's side should not bear any liability.

III. Because the plaintiff Wu Kai suffered personal injury and had to suspend his studies, although he incurred certain economic losses, among the items of compensation for personal injury provided in the Supreme People's Court's Interpretation on Several Issues concerning the Application of Law in the Trial of Cases Involving Compensation for Personal Injury, there is no item for "lost schooling expenses." Wu Kai's claim for compensation for lost schooling expenses lacks a legal basis, and therefore this claim is not upheld.

Article 106 of the General Principles of Civil Law provides: "Citizens and legal persons who breach a contract or fail to perform other obligations shall bear civil liability." "Citizens and legal persons who through their fault infringe upon state or collective property or infringe upon the property or person of others shall bear civil liability." "Where there is no fault, but the law stipulates that civil liability shall be borne, such liability shall be borne." Article 119 provides: "A person who infringes upon the person of a citizen and causes injury shall compensate for medical expenses, income lost due to lost working time, living allowances for the disabled, and other expenses; if death is caused, the person shall also pay funeral expenses, necessary living expenses for persons previously supported by the deceased, and other expenses." Paragraph 2 of Article 8 of the Supreme People's Court's *Interpretation on Issues Concerning the Determination of Compensation Liability for Mental Damages in Civil Torts* provides: "Where a tort causes mental damage to a person, resulting in serious consequences, the people's court may, in addition to ordering the tortfeasor to bear civil liabilities such as cessation of infringement, restoration of reputation, elimination of adverse effects, and making an apology, order the tortfeasor to pay corresponding moral damages compensation upon the request of the victim." Paragraph 1 of Article 10 provides: "The amount of compensation for mental damages shall be determined based on the following factors: (1) the degree of fault of the tortfeasor, unless otherwise provided by law; (2) the specific circumstances of the means, occasion, and manner of the infringement; (3) the consequences caused by the tortious act; (4) the profits gained by the tortfeasor; (5) the economic ability of the tortfeasor to bear liability; (6) the average living standard of the locality of the court hearing the case." Paragraph 1 of Article 17 of the Supreme People's Court's *Interpretation on Issues Concerning the Application of Law in the Trial of Cases Involving Compensation for Personal Injury* provides: "Where a victim suffers personal injury, the compensation obligor shall compensate for the various expenses incurred for medical treatment and the income reduced due to lost working time, including medical expenses, lost work expenses, nursing expenses, transportation expenses, accommodation expenses, hospital meal subsidies, and necessary nutrition expenses." Paragraph 2 provides: "Where the victim is disabled due to injury, the compensation obligor shall also compensate for the necessary expenses incurred due to increased living needs and the income loss caused by loss of working ability, including disability compensation, expenses for disability assistive devices, living expenses for persons supported by the victim, and rehabilitation fees, nursing fees, and subsequent treatment fees actually incurred for rehabilitation care and continued treatment." Article 18 provides: "Where the victim or the near relatives of the deceased suffer mental damage, and the compensation claimant requests the people's court to compensate for moral damages, the *Interpretation of the Supreme People's Court on Issues Concerning the Determination of Compensation Liability for Mental Damages in Civil Torts* shall apply for determination." "The right to claim compensation for moral damages shall not be assigned or inherited, except where the compensation obligor has already made a written commitment to provide monetary compensation, or where the compensation claimant has already filed a lawsuit with the people's court." Article 19 provides: "Medical expenses shall be determined based on the receipts for medical fees and hospitalization fees issued by medical institutions, in conjunction with medical records, diagnosis certificates, and other relevant evidence. If the compensation obligor disputes the necessity and reasonableness of the treatment, it shall bear the corresponding burden of proof." "The amount of compensation for medical expenses shall be determined based on the expenses actually incurred before the conclusion of the first-instance court debate. For necessary rehabilitation fees for the recovery of organ function, appropriate cosmetic surgery fees, and other subsequent treatment fees, the compensation claimant may file a separate lawsuit after the expenses are actually incurred. However, expenses that are determined to be inevitably incurred based on medical certification or expert conclusions may be compensated together with the medical expenses already incurred." Article 21 provides: "Nursing fees shall be determined based on the income status of the nursing personnel, the number of nursing personnel, and the duration of nursing." "If the nursing personnel have income, the calculation shall refer to the provisions on lost work expenses; if the nursing personnel have no income or if a hired caregiver is used, the calculation shall refer to the labor remuneration standard for caregivers engaged in the same level of care in the local area. In principle, the number of nursing personnel shall be one, but if the medical institution or appraisal institution has a clear opinion, the number of nursing personnel may be determined with reference thereto." "The nursing period shall be calculated until the victim recovers the ability to take care of himself or herself. Where the victim is unable to recover the ability to take care of himself or herself due to disability, a reasonable nursing period may be determined based on factors such as age and health condition, but shall not exceed twenty years at most." "After the victim is determined to be disabled, nursing shall be graded based on the degree of nursing dependency, in conjunction with the fitting of disability assistive devices." Article 22 provides: "Transportation expenses shall be calculated based on the expenses actually incurred by the victim and necessary accompanying personnel for seeking medical treatment or transferring to another hospital for treatment. Transportation expenses shall be evidenced by official receipts; the relevant receipts shall correspond to the location, time, number of persons, and number of trips for medical treatment." Article 23 provides: "Hospital meal subsidies may be determined with reference to the standard of meal subsidies for general staff of local state organs on business trips." "If it is truly necessary for the victim to receive treatment in another locality and he or she is unable to be hospitalized due to objective reasons, the reasonable portion of accommodation and meal expenses actually incurred by the victim and his or her accompanying personnel shall be compensated." Article 24 provides: "Nutrition fees shall be determined based on the victim's injury status, with reference to the opinion of the medical institution." Article 25 provides: "Disability compensation shall be calculated based on the degree of loss of working ability or the level of disability of the victim, calculated from the date of disability determination for twenty years, according to the per capita disposable income of urban residents or the per capita net income of rural residents in the locality of the court hearing the case for the preceding year. However, for those over 60 years of age, one year shall be deducted for each additional year of age; for those over 75 years of age, it shall be calculated for five years." "If the victim's actual income has not decreased due to disability, or if the degree of disability is relatively minor but has caused occupational impediments seriously affecting employment, the disability compensation may be adjusted accordingly." In accordance with the above provisions, the medical expenses of the plaintiff, Wu Kai, shall be determined as RMB 39,592.58; nursing fees, calculated with reference to the relevant standards of Jiangsu Province at one person for four months, shall be RMB 6,767.67; transportation expenses and accommodation expenses are determined respectively as RMB 2,040 and RMB 1,000 at the court's discretion. Wu Kai's injury constitutes a Level 10 disability, causing him certain physical and mental harm. The defendant Shuguang School and the defendant Zhu Chao shall pay moral damages to Wu Kai. Based on factors such as the degree of fault of the tortfeasors, the means, occasion, and manner of the infringement, and the average living standard of the locality of the court hearing the case, the specific amount of moral damages is determined at RMB 4,000 at the court's discretion. In addition, both parties have no objection to the compensation for hospital meal subsidies, nutrition fees, disability compensation, and appraisal fees, and these are confirmed accordingly.

Accordingly, the Chuzhou District People's Court of Huai'an City, Jiangsu Province, rendered the following judgment on December 16, 2005:

I. The medical expenses of the plaintiff, Wu Kai, in the amount of RMB 39,592.58, nursing fees of RMB 6,767.67, hospital meal subsidies of RMB 180, nutrition fees of RMB 249.37, disability compensation of RMB 9,508, transportation expenses of RMB 2,040, accommodation expenses of RMB 1,000, moral damages of RMB 4,000, and appraisal fees of RMB 300, totaling RMB 63,637.62, shall be borne by the legal representative of the defendant Zhu Chao, Zhu Shanyong, to the extent of 30%, i.e., RMB 19,091.29, and after deducting the amount of RMB 561.60 already paid, the amount to be compensated is RMB 18,529.69; and by the defendant Shuguang School to the extent of 70%, i.e., RMB 44,546.33, and after deducting the amount of RMB 10,000 already paid, the amount to be compensated is RMB 34,546.33. Both amounts shall be paid to the plaintiff Wu Kai within ten days after this judgment takes effect;

II. The other claims of the plaintiff Wu Kai are dismissed.

The case acceptance fee of RMB 2,740 and other litigation fees of RMB 600, totaling RMB 3,300, shall be borne by the legal representative of the plaintiff Wu Kai, Wu Fucheng, in the amount of RMB 280; by the legal representative of the defendant Zhu Chao, Zhu Shanyong, in the amount of RMB 820; and by the defendant Shuguang School in the amount of RMB 2,200.

After the first-instance judgment was announced, neither party appealed, and the first-instance judgment became legally effective.
